experience.linkedin_description:
I lead development on Ludwig, a practice-management platform for physiotherapy clinics in Germany and Austria. It is used day to day by 20+ therapists and holds records for more than 10,000 patients.

I built most of it from scratch: architecture, UI, frontend, backend integration, testing, deployment, and everything since. I work directly with the CEO, so requirements reach me as business problems and I turn them into something that works for people who are busy and not technical.

What is in it:
• Clinical documentation and patient records
• Appointment scheduling, recurring bookings and available time-slot calculation
• Resource management, therapist absences and waiting lists
• Statutory health insurance (GKV) invoicing
• A booking wizard practices embed in their own website
• Mobile apps for therapists

Two parts were the hard ones. Multi-tenant architecture, so one deployment serves many practices with their data properly separated. And offline-first sync with conflict handling, because a therapist in a treatment room often has no signal and still needs to write notes, and when two people touch the same record nobody's work should disappear.

I also guide a team of 3-4 engineers on our other products: a business connector, a business-card management platform, and a regional public registry. That means technical direction, code reviews, and unblocking people.

Technologies: Angular 19, Ionic 8, TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Flutter, RxJS, NgRx Signals, Tailwind CSS, Playwright, Spica (buckets and functions), PDF workflows

experience.linkedin_description:
Two and a half years building web and mobile products for clients in logistics, marketplaces, real estate and field service. I started as a developer and moved into leading a team of 5-10.

Most of my work was backend: system design, APIs and data. I built scalable APIs in Node.js and TypeScript, worked with SQL and NoSQL through TypeORM, Sequelize and Mongoose, and spent real time on the database structure before writing the code above.

The harder pieces:
• Billing systems and payment gateway integrations
• Large CSV exports that stayed fast as the data grew
• Asynchronous processing to keep heavy jobs off the request path
• File and media handling with AWS S3 and Cloudinary
• Logging and alerting through AWS SNS, so problems surfaced before clients did
• GraphQL and Google Maps API integration
• Unit tests with Jest

The products this went into:
• Atomix, a 3PL logistics and fulfilment platform. I moved billing from a third-party service in-house and made the exports fast.
• EquipX, a heavy equipment marketplace. I designed the database and built its REST APIs and image pipeline.
• SandSeekers, a Dubai real estate platform with its own CRM, pulling live feeds from Bayut, Dubizzle and Property Finder into one place.
• Rentalytics, a data platform that scrapes and structures millions of property records.
• HIS, a SaaS product for attendance and leave management, where I owned the backend.
• 99DPF, a service booking platform on web and mobile, with real-time chat, push notifications and order status.

As team lead I reviewed code, mentored juniors, joined client calls to turn vague requirements into something we could build, and planned what shipped when.

Technologies: Node.js, NestJS, Express.js, TypeScript, Python, React, Angular, Next.js, React Native, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MariaDB, Redis, TypeORM, Sequelize, Mongoose, GraphQL, REST APIs, AWS (S3, SNS), Cloudinary, Docker, Firebase, Jest

linkedin_projects.name: Ludwig Practice Suite - Healthcare Practice Management & Patient Booking Platform
linkedin_projects.description:
Ludwig is a practice-management and patient-booking platform for physiotherapy clinics in Germany and Austria. 20+ therapists use it daily and it holds records for more than 10,000 patients.

It is three products against one backend and one clinical domain model:
• A practice dashboard where therapists run their day: patient records, clinical documentation, scheduling, resource management, absences, waiting lists and statutory health insurance invoicing
• A booking wizard a practice embeds in its own website, so patients book without ever seeing Ludwig
• Mobile apps for therapists

The backend runs on Spica. I modelled the data as buckets and wrote the server-side functions the three clients run against, so the clinical rules live in one place instead of being repeated in each app.

Two parts took the most thought.

Multi-tenancy. One deployment serves many practices and each practice's data stays strictly separated. In healthcare that is not a nice-to-have, so it shaped the data model from the start rather than being added later.

Offline-first. Treatment rooms often have no signal and a therapist still has to write notes. The app keeps working offline and syncs when it reconnects, with conflict handling so that when two people have edited the same record neither one's work quietly disappears.

Scheduling has more depth in it than it looks: recurring appointments, therapist absences, room and equipment availability, waiting lists, and computing free slots across all of that fast enough to draw a calendar without the user waiting.

Technologies: Angular 19, Ionic 8, TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Flutter, RxJS, NgRx Signals, Tailwind CSS, Playwright, Spica (buckets and functions), PDF workflows

linkedin_projects.name: Atomix - 3PL Logistics & Fulfilment Platform
linkedin_projects.description:
Atomix is a 3PL logistics and order fulfilment platform for high-growth brands: inbound and outbound orders, inventory across warehouses, and the reporting the operations team runs the day on.

I worked across both sides of it, frontend and backend. Three pieces were worth doing properly.

Large data exports. They were built in one pass and started falling over as the data grew. I moved them to chunked processing with the finished file uploaded to S3, so an export completes at any size instead of timing out on the request.

Billing. It ran through a third-party service. I helped move it to an in-house system, which took out the recurring cost and put the logic somewhere we could change it.

The frontend migration from Angular Material to PrimeNG, which I led. Fewer component workarounds and a UI the team could build against faster.

Technologies: Angular, PrimeNG, TypeScript, Node.js, Express.js, Sequelize, MariaDB, Firebase, AWS S3

linkedin_projects.name: Rentalytics - Property Data Platform
linkedin_projects.description:
Rentalytics is a data platform that collects and structures millions of property records so they can be searched and worked with in one place.

I worked on both sides. On the frontend I built the React interface for browsing and managing that data. On the backend I designed the scraping and ingestion systems in Python, which is where the real problem was: at that volume, anything written the obvious way is either too slow or falls over.

Most of the effort went into asynchronous processing, so long-running jobs stay off the request path, and into tests, because a scraper that quietly drifts is worse than one that fails loudly.

Technologies: React, Next.js, TypeScript, Node.js, Express.js, Python, PostgreSQL, TypeORM, Amazon S3, Jest

linkedin_projects.name: HIS - Attendance & Leave Management SaaS
linkedin_projects.description:
HIS is a SaaS product for managing attendance and leave across an organisation: who is in, who is off, and what has been approved.

I worked on both sides, with the backend as my main responsibility. That meant the core of it, the rules that decide what a leave request is allowed to do: entitlements, approvals, balances, and the calendar all of it is calculated against.

Attendance and leave look simple from the outside and are mostly edge cases underneath, so the value was in getting those rules right rather than in the screens sitting on top of them.

Technologies: Next.js, TypeScript, Node.js, GraphQL, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, TypeORM, Jest

linkedin_projects.name: EquipX - Heavy Equipment Marketplace
linkedin_projects.description:
EquipX is a marketplace for finding and buying heavy equipment.

I worked across both sides, with most of my time on the backend. Before any code I modelled the database from an ERD, because a marketplace's listing and category structure is the one thing you cannot cheaply change later.

On top of that I built the APIs, and an image pipeline that processes uploaded product photos and generates the sizes each screen needs. Those are stored on Cloudinary, so pages stay quick on a slow connection.

The other two pieces were real-time chat with Socket.IO, so buyers and sellers talk inside the platform rather than swapping phone numbers, and Stripe payments, so a purchase completes without leaving the site.

Technologies: React, Next.js, Node.js, Express.js, MongoDB, Socket.IO, Cloudinary, Stripe, AWS

linkedin_projects.name: Definepedia - Tutoring Marketplace
linkedin_projects.description:
Definepedia is a tutoring marketplace in the mould of Chegg: students post questions, and tutors either answer them or get hired for longer help.

I built the backend from scratch. I designed the architecture and the data model in Express.js and MongoDB with Mongoose schemas, and added Stripe payments so a student can hire and pay a tutor inside the platform rather than being sent somewhere else.

Technologies: Node.js, Express.js, MongoDB, Mongoose, Stripe
